feedback: If a learner describes the flat section as 'flat ground', restate that standing still means distance is not changing even though time keeps passing.
When predictions differ, walk the journey again slowly and build the line segment by segment so the mapping is explicit.
activities.intendedInsight: Grounding the abstraction in lived motion builds the motion→line link: stopping produces a flat section, returning toward the start produces a downward slope (when distance is measured from the start), and faster walking produces a steeper line.
learnerActions: Walk a journey along a marked distance line on the floor against a timer while classmates predict the shape of the resulting graph.
Pause partway (stand still) and discuss what the line does during that pause.
Walk back toward the start and note how the graph's slope changes direction (it slopes downward because the graph shows distance from the start).
Compare a fast walk and a slow walk and connect the difference to the steepness of the segments.
activities.title: Walk the graph (embodied journey)

feedback: If a learner names the highest point as fastest, compare two segments' steepness directly: speed is steepness, not height, and the highest point may be where the object has stopped.
If a learner reads a single distance or time value and calls it the speed, point out that speed needs BOTH a change in distance and the time taken — one axis reading alone cannot give it.
Check that learners do not assume the line starts at the origin (0,0) when the object starts some way from the reference point; the line then begins partway up the distance axis.
activities.intendedInsight: Speed is read from the gradient of a segment (distance ÷ time), while the horizontal flat section means stationary; the highest point is not necessarily the fastest.
learnerActions: Before interpreting any feature, state what the vertical axis measures, what the horizontal axis measures, and what the origin represents.
Describe, stage by stage, what is happening on a given graph — moving away, stopped, returning, fast or slow.
Identify the fastest section by finding the STEEPEST segment (greatest gradient), not the highest point.
Calculate the average speed of one straight segment as distance ÷ time for that segment, using the axis scales.
activities.title: Read the axes and narrate each stage

feedback: If a learner sketches a described journey as a literal picture (a hill for speeding up), compare it to a correct concave-up curve and re-link steepness to speed.
For 'speeding up smoothly', confirm the line gets progressively steeper rather than jumping to a straight diagonal (which would be constant speed).
In a two-line comparison, confirm 'fastest' is chosen by the steeper line, not the one that reaches higher.
A vertical line (infinite speed) or a line going backwards in time is physically impossible — flag and discuss why.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent interpretation means translating in both directions between a written journey and the graph, treating the graph as an abstract distance-time relationship rather than a literal picture of the route.
learnerActions: Match journey descriptions (e.g. 'she stopped for lunch, then hurried home') to the correct graph segments or whole graphs, in small groups.
Sketch a distance-time graph from a written journey that includes stops and speed changes, including a return to the start.
Sketch the graph for a cyclist who sets off slowly and speeds up smoothly — a curve that starts shallow and gets steeper (concave up), not a straight line and not a hill-shaped picture.
Order four runners by speed by comparing the gradients of their lines.
Point to a place on your own sketch where the object is stopped and explain how the graph shows it.
activities.title: Translate both ways: match and sketch
